neutral_facts.value: The accused, Krishan, and his mother, Shardi, were prosecuted for the death of Krishan's wife, Rani, who was set on fire. Rani made a dying declaration alleging that Krishan set her on fire and that he had a history of beating her under the influence of liquor. The trial court acquitted both accused due to the hostility of key witnesses and the lack of corroboration for the dying declaration. The High Court, however, convicted Krishan based on the dying declaration, the statement of the Judicial Magistrate, and the Investigating Officer. The deceased survived for two to three days after making her statement, which was recorded in accordance with legal procedures. The medical report confirmed that Rani suffered severe burns but was fit to make her statement. The trial court found that the deceased's family members, including her father-in-law and sister-in-law, helped extinguish the fire, and Krishan was present and also suffered burns. The High Court emphasized that the dying declaration, when recorded properly, can form the basis of conviction if it is true and reliable.

quotes.text: FIR No. 134 was registered against accused Shardi and Krishan under Sections 307, 498A, 109 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short "IPC") on 30th March, 1998.
Based upon the dying declaration made by the deceased, FIR was registered under Sections 498A, 307, 109 and 34 IPC.

The Judgment of the Court was delivered by SWATANTER KUMAR, J. 1. This appeal is directed against the judgment of conviction and order of sentence dated 17th July, 2007 passed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh whereby the High Court reversed the judgment of acquittal passed by the Trial Court against the accused Krishan.
Dismissing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1. The hostility of PW1, PW3 and PW4 cannot demolish the value and reliability of the dying declaration of the deceased.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the dying declaration of the deceased, recorded in accordance with established practice and procedures, is a truthful version of the events leading to her death and can form the sole basis of conviction if it is true, reliable, and recorded properly.

quotes.text: The prosecution argued that the dying declaration of the deceased, recorded in accordance with established practice and procedures, is a truthful version of the events leading to her death and can form the sole basis of conviction if it is true, reliable, and recorded properly.

prosecution_argument.note: no quote occurs in the judgment; closest passage (p.2, match 80): "The dying declaration has been proved in accordance with law, is a truthful version of the events that occurred and the circumstances leading to her death."

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the hostility of the witnesses undermines the reliability of the dying declaration and that the prosecution failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt due to the lack of corroboration from key witnesses.

quotes.text: The Trial Court found that in the facts of the present case, it was not safe to rely upon the dying declaration of the deceased and acquitted both the accused.

The learned counsel for the accused-respondents, supporting the judgment of the trial Court, has pointed out that the benefit of doubt should be given to the husband because he was the person who tried to extinguish the fire and as a result thereof, he received burn injuries on his hands.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a dying declaration can form the sole basis of conviction if it is true, reliable, and recorded in accordance with established practice and principles, and that the hostility of witnesses is a relevant consideration but not the sole determinative factor.

quotes.text: It is not an absolute principle of law that a dying declaration cannot form the sole basis of conviction of an accused when such dying declaration is true, reliable and has been recorded in accordance with the established practice and principles.
The hostility of the witnesses is a relevant consideration, but is not the sole determinative factor for deciding the guilt or otherwise of an accused.
